content:
Hummingbirds are birds native to the Americas and comprise the biological family Trochilidae. About 366 species and 113 genera occur from Alaska to Tierra del Fuego, but the vast majority of the species are found in the tropics around the equator. They are small birds, with most species measuring 3–5 inches long. The smallest extant hummingbird species is the bee hummingbird, which is 2 inches long and weighs less than 0.07 oz; the largest hummingbird species is the 9-inch giant hummingbird, weighing 0.63–0.85 oz. They specialize in feeding on flower nectar, but all species consume flying insects or spiders. Hummingbirds separated from their sister group, the swifts and treeswifts, around 42 million years ago. The common ancestor of extant hummingbirds is estimated to have lived 22 million years ago in South America. They are called hummingbirds because of the sound created by their beating wings, which flap at audible frequencies.

Indigenous people have a variety of legends and beliefs about hummingbirds. Some groups see the small bird as a healer, spirit helper, or fire-bringer. It’s generally considered to be good luck to see a hummingbird. Some believe they’re magical creatures because they seem to appear and disappear. Others think hummingbirds can lead people through difficult challenges because they are so agile. Others view them as messengers of love, and many Native American cultures have vivid stories about hummingbirds. Most stories are wrapped into the mythology of the people. For example, Hopi and Zuni communities talk about a time of famine when a family faced starvation. The children carved a hummingbird out of wood while their parents searched for food. The bird came to life. Seeing that they were hungry, the bird flew to the center of the Earth to beg the fertility god to deliver rain so the crops would grow.

Native American tribes in the United States have traditional stories about hummingbirds. In the Pacific Northwest, tribes have hummingbird clans with the tiny bird represented on totem poles. The birds are respected as fierce fighters and territory defenders. One legend says that Raven used magic to transform a flower into a hummingbird and asked it to take a message to all of the flowers. That’s why hummingbirds flit from flower to flower—thanking each for its beauty. In the Mojave Desert, legend says people lived underground in darkness. Then, a hummingbird was sent to look for light and returned with the good news of a path to the upper world where we live now. In the Southeastern woodlands, the Cherokee remember when the evil Dagul’ku goose stole the only tobacco plant. Many animals tried to get it back but failed. A hummingbird stole seeds from the plant, so everyone had tobacco again.

The hummingbird had sacred importance in Aztec culture. Huitzilopochtli (Wheat-zee-lo-poach-tli) was the Aztec sun and war god and was portrayed as a hummingbird. Dead warriors and women who died giving birth were believed to return as hummingbirds. Huitzilopochtli was said to be in a constant struggle with the darkness and required sacrifices to ensure the sun would survive the cycle of 52 years, which was the basis of many Mesoamerican myths. Human sacrifice and self-bloodletting were key offerings to the god. He demanded blood to be appeased. So individual bloodletting became a daily rite for the Aztecs. Everyone gave blood no matter their age, gender, or social status. Animals were also regularly slaughtered. The most important act was public human sacrifice. The high priest would typically sacrifice prisoners of war with great pageantry and ritual. The human blood offered in these ceremonies was thought to postpone the world’s end.
